passages.text: During distress, prioritize safety, supervise nearby and allow time to settle. Emotion coaching waits until both people are calm (Practice emotion coaching).
passages.action: Stay nearby, check that everyone is safe, and give your child time and space. Save problem-solving for when you are both calmer.
passages.wording: I’m nearby. We can talk when you’re ready.
passages.why: Distress can make conversation difficult; waiting leaves room for listening later.

passages.text: When calm and able to engage, listen without judgment and tentatively name feelings; the child may correct the label (Steps 3–4; Reflecting emotions).
passages.action: When your child can engage, listen and gently check what they are feeling. Accept a correction.
passages.wording: It looks like something is upsetting you. Is that right?
passages.why: Listening and naming feelings can help children learn to recognize emotions.

title: Toddler Tantrums 101: Why They Happen and What You Can Do

passages.text: Prevention and Intervention: communicate necessary limits briefly and steadily; accept feelings while maintaining limits without shaming.
passages.action: If a limit is needed, state it briefly in a steady voice while acknowledging the feeling.
passages.wording: You seem upset. The limit is still the same. I’m here.
passages.why: A brief, compassionate limit can support regulation without shaming.

passages.text: Prevention: give notice before an activity ends; offer genuine, limited choices. Advance notice does not always prevent a tantrum.
passages.action: Before an activity ends, give a concrete heads-up and offer two acceptable choices when there really is a choice.
passages.wording: After this turn, we’re leaving. Would you like to walk beside me or hold my hand?
passages.why: A heads-up and a small choice may make the change easier to anticipate; they will not prevent every protest.

passages.text: Provide clear directions: describe the action wanted instead of a vague command to stop. Encourage positive choices: give two simple acceptable options.

passages.text: Tips 1–5: use a brief repeatable goodbye, give attention at parting and explain return in terms the child understands; keep the return promise.

passages.text: Be a good listener: ask about the child’s experience, listen and repeat what you understood to check meaning; agreement is not required.
passages.locator: How can I improve communications in my family? Be a good listener
passages.action: Make a little time without distractions. Listen to your child, then check whether you understood rather than assuming what they feel.
passages.wording: I want to understand. Did I get that right?
passages.why: Checking your understanding lets your child correct you and helps communication.

passages.text: Keeping Your Cool: slow breaths and a pause before talking can help a stressed adult; seek professional help if feeling out of control.

passages.wording: I need a moment to calm my voice. Then I’ll listen.
passages.why: Pausing can help you approach the conversation more calmly.
